Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: [interview begins mid-sentence]...26th, 2002 at Preferred Care, 259 Monroe Avenue in Rochester New York interviewing Vern Etshman, date of birth 6-13-26. His current address is?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: 115 Sewilo, S-e-w-i-l-o, Hills Drive, Rochester, New York, 14622.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: And the person interviewing is myself, Annette Goodman. I met Vern through the Veteran's History Project through Saint John Fisher College in Rochester, New York, and with us is?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Sarah Hannon, the volunteer for Preferred Care.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: And Vern, what war were you in?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: World War II.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: And branch of service?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: The Navy.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: And what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I was a quartermaster third class by the time I ___.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: And where did you serve?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: ___ mostly.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Could you play it back to me? Were you drafted or did you enlist, Vern?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Okay. Where were you living at the time you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: ___, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Is that where you were born?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, it was something that most of the guys in my class had done. I think at the time our class graduated there were only either one or two men left in the class, males. I obviously felt strongly about the fact that we had been attacked by another country. I wanted to get in and do my part, and I also looked forward to the chance to see the world, to get out of a little small town where -- it was a good town to come from, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You waited until you came of age to do it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You probably would have done it earlier --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes, I would have, as a matter of fact.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: And how old were you when you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Seventeen.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Seventeen. Why --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I quit high school as a matter of fact.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh, you quit high school?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Something that came back to haunt me for the rest of my life.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Why did you pick the Navy?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: It seemed to me the most attractive way to fight a war.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. Having enlisted -- I think I left on the 2nd of February, 1944, and we were training in Sampson Navy Base and it was a long -- very, very cold and windy lake, and it was one of the most horrible experiences you could have had because every day we had to go out and march in it and do all kinds of things. It was very uncomfortable being there at that time of the year. I don't remember much about our training. I remember being taught how to jump off of a ship with a life jacket on so that you wouldn't break your neck when you hit the water. I remember being taught over and over and over again how to march although I never used that after I left Sampson. That's basically all I remember about it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did they have indoor tanks in which -- into which you jumped?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We had a swimming pool -- a very large swimming pool, olympic size practically.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: How did you get through it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: My brother had been in the Navy before me, and I knew pretty well from all the things that we had talked about what he went through and I expected that's what I was going through, so it really wasn't a problem getting through it because I pretty much anticipated -

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: And you felt that you were being trained? The reason I ask is the last veteran we interviewed said he spent a good deal of his enlistment going up and down the coast being shipped here and there, and no one was giving him a job, so I was just wondering. Ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I can remember one very interesting thing. We were taught to salute anything that moved, anything that was higher than we were, and just about everyone was higher than we were, and we were told that when we got out of boot camp we didn't have to worry about saluting. For example, we didn't have to salute people in a car. We didn't have to salute people that were non-commissioned officers, things like that. One of the first assignments I got was in Norfolk, Virginia where I had to stay on the gate guard one night. I had never done that. I had no idea what I was supposed to do except I knew I was supposed open the gate, and a car came along and I opened the gate, and the car went by me, and then I closed the gate. All of a sudden the car backed up, and this back window went down and a head stuck out of the window with all kinds of scrambled eggs on the hat. It turned out one was the commandant of the base and the other was the head of the Fifth Fleet -- I'm not sure anymore -- but they were both admirals in the back seat. One admiral said to me, what's the matter, sailor, don't you know how to salute? I said yes, sir, and he said, well let me see it. Well, he had me standing there like an idiot saluting him, and then he drove away. The next thing I got word was that I had been put on report, and I had to go to a captain's mast. I was restricted. So, they lied to me. You do have to salute some people when they're in cars.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Why was he more concerned about that than --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: -- than the fact that you didn't ask for identification, did you?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I say, you didn't ask them for identification, they just drove through?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You were required to do that?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That wasn't the problem. Of course, the car was filled with Navy people, so I guess I hadn't thought about that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: That's interesting.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That was not a good start.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Hitler could have been in the back seat, you know.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. I could handle Hitler. It was the admiral I didn't know what to do about.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Where did you go from Sampson?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I went to anti-submarine warfare training program in Key West, Florida. From the cold to the hot, and we had simulated submarine training attacks. You would sinter the sonar equipment just as you would on a ship, and there was a screen being run by somebody else, and they would manipulate a submarine, and our job was to try to catch them, track them down, and blow them up.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Radar?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, sonar.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh, sonar, sorry.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: In addition to working in simulators we also went out in the submarine chasers and what they used to call yag boats. They were converted yachts. The sonar equipment was down in the bilges of the ship, and most of us got sea sick before we even got out of port. We used to go out every morning. We had breakfast down there, and between the diesel oil slopping around and the movement of the ship most of us were sick before we even started. That was an interesting experience too because there were sailors there from almost every one of the allied countries. We trained with Russians and Cubans and French, Norweigian, Canadians, Australians, and they all had their own ships, and the Russians were very playful. We used to love to ___ as close to us as they could get and make our captain nervious, which he got nervous quite frequently. So, our training was both on ships and on land.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, what was your exact -- once you got done with that you were working on the sonar, what was your assignment once you --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, after we completed sonar training we went to Norfolk where we were to undergo destroyer training, and I looked forward to that because I used to get so sick on the little boats that we went out on I thought being on a destroyer would be like being on a battle ship. It turned out that wasn't true either. They have a different motion, but they have almost every bit as much motion. So, we had to learn how to sail without getting sick, and we never did quite until we were out for a long, long time. Anyway, we would then go out on assignments and do all kinds of things with our destroyer, learning how to do our particular jobs on that particular ship. Most of the people with whom we trained were going to be on the ship that was ___ so it was at that point learning how to do our job, a group of people who would ___.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Then from there we were -- we went to Chickasaw, Alabama where our ship was being built, and we put the ship into commission. Then we went back up the east coast and we went back and forth to places like Bermuda doing a shake-down cruise to learn the ship. That meant putting the ship through all kinds of -- all kinds of crazy stuff.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Now, what kind of ship was this?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: It was a destroyer.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: A destroyer.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: All my career was on destroyers, and they would do everything they could to make the ship -- make something happen to it, because once we were assigned out in combat we wanted to make sure that our ship would respond to every command that we gave it, and any problem that we would have that we were able to pin them down before we left the country. It was quite an arduous operation. We went to Bermuda to do that. We would make runs on regular submarines, go through simulated combat with other ships. You know, we would go as fast as we possibly could. Open your ship wide up, see how fast it would go, and then slam on ___ brakes, but things ___ see how quickly we could stop, how quickly we could turn, how fast we could go and still turn without having to worry about it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: How long does it take a ship to stop?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I don't remember. This is a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I really don't remember. I know we always stopped when we had to though.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: What was the name of your ship?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: The U.S.S. Van Valkenburgh. The ship was named after the captain of the battleship Arizona that was sunk at Pearl Harbor, and it's still there, both Van Valkenburgh and the ship.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: So, did you eventually see combat? We've been going through all the training missions so far.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. A little side line, if I can. Do you want side lines or do you just want --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Sorry?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: So, do you want little side lines or do you just want --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Everything, everything.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I went through boot camp with a fellow who was a very good friend of mine, and he and I were right next to each other alphabetically, and we went from Sampson. We also went to Key West for destroyer -- group training, and he went with me to Norfolk for training on destroyers, and then when the ship assignment came up we were hoping that we would be together again, and we weren't. He was assigned to one destroyer. I was assigned to another one. When we went to the Pacific he never quite got where we were going because his ship had sunk on the way over. I wish he had gotten on my ship. I'm glad I didn't get on his. So, it kind of started very quickly.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You got to the Pacific through the canal?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We went through the Panama Canal, yes. That was quite a good experience too. There's nothing like being up in the top of a mountain in a ship looking down, going through the forest in a ship. For a ___ from Pennsylvania it was quite exciting.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: So, where did you go once you got to the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, we went to Pearl Harbor, and we joined some of the other ships that were going to be in our division, and then we learned to work together. Then we took off -- we stopped at a little island called Little Wetok on the way over. That's the only stop I remember going over.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You didn't encounter any combat on the ocean?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, not at that point we didn't, no, because the Japanese had already been chased ___ there, although there was a battle before we even got there. We went directly to Saipan, and we spent time in Saipan ___. I remember I was assigned to a crew that was supposed to go ashore and bring back ammunition, and there were still Japanese snipers in the forest that we had to go through to get there, so I learned how to get scared rather quickly, and I was scared, but we got back safely. Anyway, from Saipan we then went on to the battle of Iwo Jima. That's what we were getting ready for bringing all the ships together. So, Iwo Jima was my first real battle.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Now, the ships were basically to protect the landing of troops, is that it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Destroyers are designed to do a lot of things. They are designed to protect other ships -- other large ships. Since they had the capacity to track down submarines and blow them up hopefully we would go ahead of convoys and make sure that the convoys weren't attacked by submarines. That was one of our functions. We were also used for bombardment. Whenever we were in combat we would go up as close to the beach as we could get. I remember at Iwo Jima we were -- the captain asked for our depths, and the fellow said 22-something, and the captain said fathoms, and the guy says no, feet. We were almost touching the bottom. That's how close we were to the beach. So, we did a lot of close combat support when the Marines were moving up to the fire ahead of us ___ the Japanese that were ahead of us. In fact, I remember one day one of the Marines hollering "hey, you're shooting our own people here", in quotes. We were also used for anti-aircraft work. There were other things that were assigned to us with whatever happened. We'd go behind aircraft carriers, and if a ship [sic] missed the carrier and went into the ocean we would try to pick up the surviving pilot. If the Japanese were to fire a torpedo at a ship, like a battleship or an aircraft carrier it would be our job to get between the torpedo and the ship and take it ourselves, because there were only 330 of us on our ship, and there were hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of people on the larger ships, so in that respect we were sacrificial lambs.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did you take any torpedos?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. We've had them go around us, over and under us -- or under us and around us, but never hit us.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did the Japanese fire on the ship outside of torpedoes? Did they fire on the ship from the land?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: One day we were right up close to the beach at Iwo Jima, and all of a sudden tracer bullets started coming towards us, and that's kind of scary because I was a look-out, and I was standing there looking right at them coming right at me. If you've never seen a tracer bullet come at you ___ it's quite an experience. So, we just started firing on them. They stopped, and I guess _____ hit. But yeah, we were shot at by the shore. We also attacked a submarine on the way over to Iwo Jima. I was on the sonar equipment one night and got a sonar contact. I notified the captain, and he told the fleet commander, and they took the whole fleet and went off in a different direction, and left us out there to track down the submarine, and we knew for sure who batted or not. They disappeared after we dropped depth charges on them, but it was nighttime and we had no way of knowing that we got it or not, so I don't know what happened. I'd like to think I got them.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Now, what happens when, say -- because you were the first initial person to see the contact with that submarine, what happens? Would someone else come in and take control at that point or --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. Sonar equipment is always manned by two people. There were two different aspects to the equipment, and if you were the sonar man who made contact with a submarine then you were the one who had a responsibility for that. If there were general courier calls, since only two men could be on it -- there were two men assigned; our senior sonar man and another fellow. My job during general couriers was to be a starboard look-out. I was to look for anything; ships, planes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: While you were doing that somebody was still manning the sonar?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Somebody was still manning the equipment, that's right. The only time the sonar equipment was not being used was when, for some reason or other, we would be going over a certain speed. I think it was 30 knots as I recall. If you go over 30 knots it was not possible to use the sonar equipment because of the sound of the water rushing _____.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Were you ever a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. Are you ___ tese questions? I was talking about an experience we had. At one time for some reason -- I think it was because one of the supply ships either had been sunk or something had happened to it -- for quite a long period of time we ate nothing but rice for breakfast, dinner, supper, everything, and all of us, of course, were very, very sick of rice, and one of the times I wrote home to my mother I made the comment that when I came home I never wanted to be served rice, and that was all I said about it. Mother, getting the letter, thought I wonder if he's trying to tell me in code that he's a prisoner of the Japanese because all he's doing is eating rice.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: A good assumption.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I hadn't thought that she might have interpreted that, but anyway that was her very real fear until she got my next letter, and those were usually at least a month apart if not more because mail's ___ is not very good out there. Another thing that goes along with that, when we were finally done -- got our food back we were on a mission down off the coast of Formosa that's now Taiwan, but we were supposed to look at Japanese evacuating from Formosa, and any ships that we saw would probably be Japanese ships, and we would destroy them. So, we went down there pretty much by ourselves. I don't know if there was other ships with us. I don't recall any other ships. But we had a dot on our radar screen, and we went after it, and it turned out to be a small fishing boat. Two fishermen were in it, and we had a fellow on our ship who could speak ___. We asked them if they had seen any Japanese ___. They hadn't. But when we left they were very scared because they thought we were going to sink them. We were headed right for them with our guns pointed at them.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: A fishing boat and a great big ___.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: So, when we left we gave them a couple of big tureens filled with rice.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You got rid of your rice.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And as we were leaving we looked back and the two fellows had looked at the rice, they tasted it, and they threw it over the side. They didn't eat it. That was kind of comical because even they wouldn't eat our rice, but we were supposed to.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, you actually missed spam, is that it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I missed spam. I don't ___ spam. There were some meals I would get up early in the morning for, and that was Spam and pancakes.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Were there many casualties in your unit or your fleet? I guess, how many ships are even in a fleet?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: During the battle of Iwo Jima, no. Are we done with Iwo Jima? I'd like to go back and tell you one thing. I was the look-out, and I was right next to the beach, and I saw the flag go up on Mount Suribachi, that very famous picture that -- actually I don't know if that was the one they took a picture of. It was up and then it came down, and then it went back up again, and I saw it both times, and from my position being able to see it I announced to the crew the flag had gone up over Suribachi. Every time I see that, of course, I -- so, back in Iwo Jima.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I heard about the flag going up and then coming down. A friend of mine was in the ____ as a photographer, and he told me the initial flag raising was re-enacted for the picture. In other words, the picture was not the picture of the actual first flag raising.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: They asked them to re-enact it, yes, so that's probably what you saw.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That's probably what I saw; a fake flag raising.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yeah. Well, you saw the original one, and then it came down and --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Well, no doubt your interpretation when it came down was my goodness, they've recaptured it, or what?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, they had just taken the mountain. That's why the flag went up, and I didn't know who else might be out there besides the fellows who took them out. The Japanese were everywhere. They had tunnels all over that island, and -- you know, our troops would go by it, and then all of a sudden they would get in back of our troops.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I remember some time in the fifties they discovered -- and I don't know if it was on Iwo Jima or the other islands -- they discovered a number of Japanese who didn't even know the war was over.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That was in Guam I believe.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Was it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Was it Guam?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I'm not sure, but these men had been living on the island.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No one ever told them the war was --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes, I remember that now. That was about ten years ago -- or 15 years ago. Was it more than that?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I think so. I think it was in the fifties or sixties. I may be wrong, but it was an interesting --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, life's gone so fast for me it very well might have been 30 years ago.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Anyway -- but --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: So, we were talking -- were there casualties, so --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We had no casualties. The Navy didn't take much of a beating at Iwo Jima. It was the Marine Corp that suffered all the casualties.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Our casualties came in at the battle of Okinawa, and that was, from what I understand, one of the largest beatings the United States Navy's ever taken in terms of ships lost, sailors killed or wounded. There were, I understand, close to 5,000 sailors -- destroyer sailors -- killed in that battle, and there were close to 5,000 of them wounded. We lost many, many ships. In fact, there was some concern that they were going to pull the Navy out because we couldn't afford to keep on losing so many ships. We were very -- that was quite a battle. It's probably the worst battle the Navy's ever had, and it was a weird battle. We had -- there were so many Japanese bombers coming in and bombing our ships in the harbor, and they decided that the only way they could stop that was by having radar screens far away from the island so that we could intercept the Japanese before they got to the island to bomb, and the way they decided to do it was to put destroyers on what came to be known as radar picket duty, and there were two destroyers in each picket unit, and we were all around the island just about out of sight of each other but within radar range, so we were able to cross radar. So, it made a screen and any ships -- or any planes coming down from Japan or anywhere else we would pick up on our radar. It was very successful, and in order to combat that the Japanese began using kamikaze planes, suicide planes. Their job was to come in and sink the destroyers or put them out of action so that the bombers could then come in undetected, and it was there that we had the majority of our casualties at Okinawa because the Japanese were just -- it never ended, day and night, day and night, they would -- that's the only thing you don't like to talk about.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And I have plenty of pictures of those ships and what they looked like when they were hit. An example, our ship was the only one of two I understand that went through the entire battle without getting hit or sunk, and our captain seemed to have a talent in knowing how to deal with it. We had a ship come over -- a destroyer -- that had been in the Atlantic Ocean that came over to the Pacific but we needed more help. More destroyers were being put out of commission so fast and the other captain was superior to ours in rank. That rank -- as I understand the theory of ranking here if you were both in the same class at Annapolis and one graduates fifth in the class and the other graduates sixth the guy who was fifth is superior to the guy who graduated sixth, and he's in command, and this guy apparently was superior to my captain, but he had never fought the kamikaze planes. So, he ordered our ship -- he said well, we are under attack. He said we will do this and this and this, and my captain called back and he said if we're under attack get the hell out of my way, and we were attacked and the other ship got hit, and we didn't. He ended up having to go save them because they were sinking and they had a lot of casualties. My captain had a good instinct. We learned to sleep standing up because you never knew when they were coming. In fact I slept through an air raid one time I was so tired. Not one of my better moments. We often went for hours and hours and days sometimes without sleeping.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: So, what were your shifts like on the --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Four on, four off, and when you went on general quarters you were on until it was over. So, if you were on for four hours and then you went to general quarters when you got off general quarters hours later it may be time for your shift again, and you went back on shift. It really wares you down, plus all the tension and the ___ not knowing from one minute to the next whether you were going to be alive or dead.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: How did you cope with that feeling of not knowing whether you'd be alive or dead?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, as I said before, I'm somewhat of a ___. I feel if it's going to happen it's going to happen, and if I can't do anything about it then I'm not going to worry about it. I only tend to worry when there's something I can do about it. So, I accepted the fact. I always figured that I probably would die. It was just -- the only thing that scared me was wondering how I was going to do it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: That's what I was wondering, fear -- you know.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Being -- well, there were a lot of ways that a destroyer person can -- you could be hit by the ship or the plane itself. It could land on you or near you and blow you up. If the ship sinks and you happen to be in a locked place as most of our sailors were, on the decks, fellows that were putting up ammunition or the guys who were running the ship down in the engine rooms. When the ships would sink they would go down with the ship which is a horrible way to go because you're alive, you're entombed in the ship, and you know you're not going to get out. It's just a matter of going down, down, down, and dying as you're going. That's kind of scary. Also I used to worry about being in the ocean, wondering who down there was waiting to nibble on my feet. That was scary too. My prayers were not keep me alive, they were help me to cope with whatever happens, and that's exactly what I did. I prayed a lot, but I guess I accepted fate.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did you find this was true of most of the men in ___?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: The alternative is to get hysterical, I guess.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That's right, and you can't. You all depend on each other to stay alive. This is like a football team. If you don't work together you're not going to win, and we did, which is all the result of all the training we got before we went out, learning to work together as a crew. As I told Annette earlier, our crew was made up of sailors who had come from other ships. They brought in the experience, and then young guys like me who had never done it were to learn from them, and before we went into combat the other guys wanted to make sure that they could trust us to do what had to be done. So, in a sense they took the boys -- I guess it is -- out of us. If we acted like kids and did silly or dumb things they let us know that they didn't like it, we should stop doing it. I can remember one guy they threw overboard one time because he was always mouthing off to the other guys. So -- you know, you came to depend on each other.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: From Okinawa where did you go after that?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: From Okinawa we were supposed to go on rest and rehabilitation down in Australia, and that was just wonderful. We thought this is going to be great, going to Australia. We all heard abut Australia. But in route to Australia they changed our orders and we went to the Philippine Islands instead and our job then was to start preparing the invasion of Japan. That wasn't very nice. The Philippines were kind of a dumpy place, although we only got to shore one night.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Just one night when you were there?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We were -- they divide the ship up into, like, port and starboard or something like that, and they might give port the night out to go out on leave or something. The starboard says there and takes care of the ship, and I think they gave one leave one time. We could go in and have a beer party, but a number of guys on our ship decided they wanted to get boring. Some sailors are very motivated to find women, and these fellows were so motivated, and they stole a whale boat, and the captain's gig, and pushed them as far as they could push them, and then the started the motors and went into the Philippines -- a little town on the island somewhere, and one of the guys was called for some reason, and he didn't respond. They went looking for him and they found out he wasn't there. Then they found out a few other guys weren't there. Then they found out that the boats had been stolen, so all the hands were called up on deck. We were -- some of us were asleep. They woke us up, and we had to go up on deck and stand there and freeze until these guys come swimming back pushing the boats. That was a fun night too. I mean, that's kind of a turn on. The captain put them all on report. They all had a captain's mast. Most of them he demoted in rank. That was their punishment. There were some things I can't tell you. It was an experience. That was the only fun we had in the Philippines. After that we got a variety of assignments. One of somebody had an idea -- I'll put that one away. One of the things that we did -- our ship was set up to the coast of Japan -- close to the coast of Japan -- our ship alone, and our job was to try to find any Japanese ships in the area. Preparatory to invading the island they wanted to know how many warships there were around, and we were told that anything we found we were to sink because it would be an enemy. We had a radar contact one night. It looked like on radar to be something about the size of a destroyer, and it was running pretty well parallel to us but behind us -- no, ahead of us. We went to general quarters and I was a look-out, and the captain kept saying it's right out there, see it? I said no, sir, I can't see it. God damn it boy, it's right out there. I said I can't see it, captain. He became more and more agitated, walking back and forth, back and forth. Then he'd ask me again, and now, here we are not far from Japan and we're the only American ship up there, and the one thing you wanted to do is always to maintain darkness because a light could be seen miles and miles and miles away. Our captain got so frustrated. We kept getting closer and closer and we still couldn't see it. So the captain -- we had all our guns aimed at it, all our torpedoes aimed at it, and we had big huge spot lights that were aimed at it, but not turned on. Everything was done by radar, so we all --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did it show up on radar?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. This is what we were following on radar.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Even though you couldn't see it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Even though I couldn't see it. So, finally the captain said prepared to illuminate, and prepare to fire, and we turned on the spot lights and there was a whole flock of pelicans lying along side of us.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: That would have been --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That was fun.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: That would have been overkill.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And we exposed ourselves for a flock of pelicans, but fortunately apparently nobody saw us.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Nobody responded?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. Another thing after Okinawa -- someone had gotten the idea to send ships up the Yangtze River and bomb part of Shanghai, and we were ___.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Would the river take ships that size?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Shipping ___. So, there were a couple of destroyers and a couple of cruisers that were to go, and we were assigned to go up at a particular time, and then they canceled, and then they assigned us another date. When the date came they cancelled it again, and then the reassigned it, and between the time that we were to do it the Americans dropped a bomb on Hiroshima.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I was wondering if that was the --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And I suspect that the reason that they kept putting it off is because they were going to do it, they knew it. They weren't sure -- you know. The purposes of our going up ___ was nothing more than to show the American forces we had the ability to do it, and they were going to show them we could. George Busch was running the war at that time.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: But we never did get up there. Those are the kind of things that were going on after the ___. We were getting close to the -- what would have been the invasion. I think the invasion of Japan was supposed to take place in September, and we were supposed to invade an area called Sasebo, S-a-s-e-b-o. Sasebo was a Navy town. The Japanese have a large number of ships there. I have some pictures of them. They had an inner harbor and an outer harbor. The harbors were aligned with tunnels which would have been used against us if we tried to get in -- our ships. When we went into Sasebo we dropped anchor in the outer harbor, and our other ships that were with us dropped their anchors, and we spent the night there, and of course when you're on an anchor you just sort of go with the water. Whichever way the water goes you circle around with it. The next morning when we were able to see it turned out that the mines had been swept out of the harbor, and we could have taken a mine any time while we were ___.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: My goodness. Were there many casualties on ___?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: There was only one casualty on my ship -- two of them actually. One of them was war related and the other one wasn't. One time when our captain was on a mission somewhere -- I don't know. He'd take off, and we never knew where he was going or who he was going to see, and the coxswain of the whaleboat when he was bringing the captain back was coming in a little too fast and in order to stop the boat and keep it from hitting the side he put his foot out to push off, and he broke his ankle. We were about to go out on radar picket duty, and the captain didn't want anybody on the ship who wasn't able to do his job and to take care of himself, so the captain sent him over to a hospital ship to wait until his ankle got better. So, we went off to the radar picket duty. Of course we came through it unscathed, but the Japanese suicide plane landed on the deck of the hospital ship, and our friend was up there on top waiting for the ___. The other casualty was a fellow -- after the war was over -- all through the war -- apparently he used to play around with women all the time -- a very unfaithful husband, and he swore that if he ever came through the war alive he would never look at another woman besides his wife. As soon as we got back to San Diego he went out looking for a woman, he found one. She was working in concert with a couple of fellow and they found his body floating in the bay the next day. So, those two men died.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Now, he was attacked, you say in San Diego was it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah. Apparently some woman and a couple of guys worked together. They'd get a guy out by himself somewhere and strip him of his money and they'd kill him. San Diego is a tough town.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Probably because of the presence of all the vulnerable sailors there and so on.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We sailors could re-change everything -- the tone of the town. I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or ___?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah. You want to talk anymore about the ship itself perhaps?

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: I'd like to hear everything.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Anything, yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Our ship came back from Japan on what they used to call the red carpet. Every ship that came back was required to bring back Army people, Marines, or whatever. It was a means of getting them back to the States. We had a group of Marines who were very cocky and very sarcastic about our role in the war because we could sleep in a bunk at night. We could eat at a table when they had all this tough living arrangements, And nobody on the ship liked them, so on the way back we went through some terrible storms. We went through a place called the Bandino Straits which are always in turmoil. It's where a lot of different water things come together, ___, big waves and all that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: By that time you were over your seasickness, right?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: But they weren't.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: But they weren't, yeah. The wished that they could die all the way back to the States. They were just so unhappy and they didn't get much sympathy from anybody. Now, I started out to tell --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Were there any other experiences on your ship, or duties that were --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I just have to think. Could you stop that for a minute or something? I don't know. If I had any medals?

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah, I did get a few.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Is that stopped?

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: No, I didn't put the pause -- yeah, I was trying to get the pause down.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I have the World War II Victory Medal. I have the American Campaign Medal. I have the Asiatic/Pacific Campaign Medal with three bronze starts. I have the Navy Occupation Service Medal with Asia clasp. I have the Navy Unit Commendation Ribbon. I have the Combat Action Ribbon. I think that was it.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Do you remember how you got them, or was it any specific --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, I don't. Somebody sitting around deciding that whatever we did deserved a medal. I can tell you why I got the Commendation Medal if you want to hear that.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: The Commendation reads as follows: "For outstanding heroism in action in the fight or direction ship under radar picket station during the Okinawa Campaign from April 1st to June 24, 1945. "A natural and frequent target for heavy Japanese aerial attacks while occupying the advanced and isolated stations, the U.S.S. Van Valkenburgh defeated all efforts of enemy, kamikazes and dive-bombing planes to destroy her. "Constantly vigilant and ready for battle she sent out early air warning and provided fighter direction, and with her own gunfire downed four hostile planes, probably destroyed or shared in the destruction of two others, and routed many more. "On four occasions she went to the rescue of stricken ships the radar picket screen picking up survivors, aiding with the casualties, fighting fires, and controlling damages. This fight regained her to herself from subsequent surprise attacks. "A gallant fighting ship, the Van Valkenburgh, her officers, and her men withstood the stress and peril with vital radar picket duty to prevent the Japanese from striking in force against the Naval forces off the Okinawa beachhead achieving a distinctive combat record which attests the teamwork, courage, and skill of the entire company, and enhances the finest tradition of the United States Naval Services." That's why I got that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: How did you ward off kamikaze planes? You shot them out of the sky?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We shot them out of the sky. As a matter of fact someone -- and I've met a couple of the people. One was a teacher at the college I went to later when I got out of the service. I quit high school. ___ into college, and one of the teachers in our physics department was one of the men who was instrumental in developing what they call the BT fuse.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: The BT --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: -- fuse, and I also met a couple of men at Kodak who were involved with that too. The BT fuse -- and I can't tell you how it worked. I can only tell you that it worked. If a plane were coming at you, and you fired this bomb at them it didn't have to hit them. The vibrations or electric -- something from them would cause the ___ to blow up, and the Japanese would fly right into it. If you missed the plane but you were close to it it would still blow up. So, all you had to do in many cases was to get near it to blow them up. Now, to get near them was the problem. The -- the planes would come in at different ways. Some would come in very high, then come right down at us. Some would get in back of us. They'd follow the water, or even the side of us or anywhere, in front of us, and they would just come along the water --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: In which case your guns wouldn't help.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they helped. Oh, yeah. We could anything from water level on straight up.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: It went down towards the water.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, again, though, our ships are not so high that the guns are far above the water, so that you're almost shooting straight out. So, they would dive down at you at an angle, and all we had to do was to get near them, but we had to do it fast enough. The first time we were ever under attack I was the starboard lookout, and I saw a suicide plane coming right at us, and I just stood there and looked at it. I was frozen. I couldn't talk, and a guy next to me -- one of the gunners -- hit me on the back and pointed up, and there was another one coming in at a different direction. I then found my voice, but that was the first time I was under attack, and I was just ___. You know, when you see somebody coming at you in a big way and you know they're going to keep right on coming at you until they hit you, it's kind of scary.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yes. I take it they were both shot down?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. We were attacked by four little planes. One night when the one was coming in at the other side of the ship I was over as starboard lookout pretty much by myself. It was dark ___+, and the rest of the crew was on the other side of the ship. I was standing there just looking down at the water waiting for the shooting to stop, and a torpedo went right under us. He dropped a torpedo before we shot anyway. It's something you have to deal with. You become ___ and then do what you have to do, but I did ___+. You can't pray for God to save you. You've got people dying all around you. You wonder why would he even want to do that to me, and why did he do that to ___. So, that never ___.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, in case -- Praise the Lord and Pass the Ammunition, right?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. They then told me to ___+ I have.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: That was a popular song during the war.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. Praise the Lord and pass the ammunition, ___+ something to do with tradition.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: It's a British song, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Was it? I didn't know that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: It seems to me like it might have been. Anyway --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: All I know is that first line.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Well, then it ended and we'll all go home.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: That was the end of it. (END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE)

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: -- I guess personified our age was that kind -- lullabies, love songs, or songs to stimulate your patriotism, and --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: There was also satire. Remember when the Fuhrer says --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes, there was. There was a lot of satire too, yeah. Americans have a good sense of humor even during war. But, one of the reasons I think even I today have a hard time listening to some of the modern music, it's just so completely different from what I grew up with. I can't make myself like it. I mean, I have good -- I try.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I understand from my daughter there's a revival of swing.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, maybe we'll work our swing back to the good old days. I just can't imagine sitting on the front porch and rocking and listening to the music nowadays.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: No. So, what are your -- did you actually see -- you already mentioned this -- did you actually see the Japanese surrender?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I didn't see the surrender, no, but we were pretty sure it was going to happen because we had dropped two bombs at that point, and we were harbored in Buckner Bay in Okinawa with a lot of ___ ships, and when the word finally came through that the war had ended everybody started shooting. Guns were going off all over.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Just in the sky?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: In the sky, yeah, not on the ship. Finally incoming planes were screaming around us -- you know, stop shooting, stop shooting. We're up here -- you know? But all the Japanese apparently didn't know that the war had ended because a Japanese torpedo -- one of the ships in the harbor right near us -- the Battleship Pennsylvania -- and as I recall the stern sank. It wasn't that deep in the bay, but the Japanese hadn't all gotten the word to stop the war. So, we didn't know if the war was going continue or not. That night we didn't stop. It was a wild night.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, the ship didn't defend itself because --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: It didn't because we didn't -- you know, we thought there was no reason to because the war was over, and that's it. Some of the Japanese ___ apparently thought well, I'm going out and shoot.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did you participate in the Occupation?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah. There was a -- well, first of all we went to Sasebo. I mentioned that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Swinging around in the harbor. From Sasebo we were -- I can't remember the sequence. They wanted to send a couple -- they wanted to send a hospital ship up to Nagasaki because there was a prisoner of war camp near there, and they wanted to make sure that it would be all right to bring a -- one of our hospital ships up there. So, we and another ship -- another destroyer -- were the first ones to go up. You could go up the river to get there. I was one of the ones that was selected to ___ around ___+, and we went both by boat and by jeep. It was still burning. There were still bodies, and it was --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: There was no protection for you against radiation?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: There was no protection at all. In fact, I have a letter from -- well, I talk about that. Anyway, that was our responsibility; to check out Nagasaki and see if it was safe. It was safe from a combat point of view. It turned out it was not very safe from radiation. A lot of the fellows from our ship who have died -- and most of them are dying off ___+. Most of us have died from cancer. I have had cancer two different times -- three different times since 1987 or '88. In fact, I was just cleared of one cancer a couple of months ago, so I've beaten the odds. I think that was it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: How did those prisoners of war survive?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: They weren't in Nagasaki.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: They were near Nagasaki, and they were going to be brought out from the -- but they weren't at Nagasaki.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: These were Americans and British and so on and so forth?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: They were Russians, Chinese. As I remember there were a couple of nuns and a priest, Australians, and non of them ___+. Actually, Nagasaki, as bad as it was bombed, wasn't as bad as some of the other cities.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: When our planes attacked some of these cities they really blew them up. Nagasaki was especially ___. There was just one bomb that hit it.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Then we also went over to Wakayama. The greatest thing I remember about Wakayama was that they took a landing craft and brought all of the prostitutes out of Wakayama, and took them off somewhere. I don't know where it was, but they didn't want them to be there when we were there.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: These were all the what?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Prostitutes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: The Japanese kept themselves well supplied. I don't know if they were Japanese or Americans.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: ___+ Koreans ___?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes, they did. They took them from other countries. Korea, I guess, was -- ___+.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: They're still fighting that battle.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And they should.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: There were so many atrocities committed against other countries by the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: They did terrible things in China before we got into the war.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I still have difficulty buying into the Navy of Japan, but the reality is you have to.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: How did you go about staying in touch with your family? I know you said you wrote your mother.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah, that was basically all the writing -- well, I had a girlfriend that we had decided to leave -- or to breakup before I left. I didn't know how long I'd be gone. She was of a different faith, and that was causing problems for both our families, so when we left we decided that that would probably be it, but we did keep in touch after that. My mother got the good balance of the mail. I did get one letter from my brother. My brother was also over in the Pacific. He knew I was at Iwo Jima at the time I was there, and I was his baby brother. His letter to me wasn't -- he just couldn't imagine his baby brother going through what we were going through over there, so he just couldn't wait to see me again after the war ended because he wanted to get to know me, which he did. He's now 81. I just talked to him a couple days ago. He's still chugging along.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, you ___ the ___+?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. There was a style of enlistment called the duration and six. I don't know how official that was, but that's what we used to call it. When you enlisted you enlisted for the duration of the war plus six months. If the war lasted six months you would be out in a year. If the war lasted ten years you'd get out in ten years and six months. ___+ and took your chances. So, I had two and a half years, because the war ended two years earlier -- at least my service did.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Was your brother discharged during the same time you were?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. He was badly wounded. In fact, he's blind in one eye as a result of it. He was in the Naval Hospital in Chicago. I was, at that time, on another destroyer, and that ship was down in Charleston, South Carolina. I had a ruptured appendix which my officers on the Navy ship refused to acknowledge because they thought I was trying to shirk duty. They didn't ___ me, and they told me that I would have to do what I was supposed to do, which was unload ammunition from the ship. If I didn't do it I would be -- if I didn't do it that would be all right if I had appendicitis. If I didn't have appendicitis I would be court-martialed for shirking duty. So, I didn't know. I never had appendicitis before, so I unloaded all the -- you know, I took -- unloaded ammunition along with the rest of the crew, and then I was assigned to watch that night from 4:00 until midnight, and about o'clock at night I was in pain. I went into the officer of the watch, and I used a few profane words and said -- you know, I was told that I didn't have appendicitis, and I said if I don't have appendicitis I've got something, and I've get back to -- I've got to go to the hospital. So, he said okay, I'll give you a slip. I had to walk to the hospital, and I got about half way there, and I couldn't think. Someone --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: What was the distance?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, a little over a mile. Someone called an ambulance. They took me to the hospital, and the doctor looked at me and he said get this kid in the operating room immediately, and as I got on the operating table my stomach was -- so, I never got back to the ship. I was discharged right from the hospital, and my brother and I both got out about the same time, got home at the same time. Did a lot of drinking. We didn't know what else to do in civilian life. We had ___+.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did you take advantage of the G.I. Bill of Rights?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You went to college?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: The girl that I was going with at the time -- I had no intention to go to college. In my town the only people that went to college were ministers', lawyers', and doctors' sons. Everybody else worked for the railroad or did something else. I never thought about going to college, but I fell in love with a girl who was going to Drexel in Philadelphia, and she was in her third year. I had malaria plus the appendicitis problem, and weight pounds when I came home. I looked terrible. My skin was yellow. I was gaunt. In fact, I have a picture of what I looked like. I was even worse than that. And her mother said don't fool around with him, don't marry him, because he's never going to amount to anything, and that upset me, and it upset me so much that I started applying to colleges, and everybody turned me down because I hadn't graduated from high school, and I was a Lutheran, and I applied to a Lutheran college -- Muhlenberg College in Allentown, Pennsylvania, and they said if you can pass the college entrance board exam we'll take you, and they arranged for me to take it up at Cornell because I lived in that ___+ Cornell ___. I must have aced it because they accepted me.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I thought most colleges were being much more permissible with homecoming G.I.s.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: But that ___ didn't finish high school.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: But even if you didn't finish high school I'm sure they could have given you the kind of exam to see if you --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, they didn't need the ___. All the school did was ___ of application, and they didn't have any trouble with the students. Anyway --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, what did you major in?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Psychology. I had a minor in English and a minor Religion. When I got there I decided I wanted to go into the ministry, and I had been reading a lot about psycho-religious counseling. I decided that that would be something I would really enjoy doing. So, when I got out of college and went down to apply at the seminary they didn't want to take me because they needed ministers so badly -- preachers, people who could take over congregations. And I said that's not what I want to do. One of the ministers said -- you know, if you've got a calling you'll go where you're called, and I said well, this is my calling, and this is where I'm called to go, and it's not -- we're not going to make it, so I didn't go. I ultimately became a psycho-religious counselor.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes, and I was also on the board of directors for the pastoral counseling center in Rochester.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: And you're still doing that or --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. I'm retired. I've heard enough problems.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, you married the young woman at Drexel?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. As a matter of fact we were having some problems because I was -- I really was hurt by the fact that her family was fighting our marriage and she wasn't fighting her family more than I thought she should, and I invited her up for the junior prom. She said she would come. I said we've got to talk. We talked all one night. The next night was the dance, and I got very sick at the dance. I had an attack of malaria. One of my close friends who had been a Navy corpsman took me back to the campus and he nursed me through the attack of malaria. But, anyway, Jeannette was stuck there for almost a day without anybody to talk to or anything to do. I couldn't do a thing with her. I was a terrible sight, and we didn't see each other ___+. We had decided that that was probably was ___+. But, before that happened I met another girl through a blind date, and I liked her. She like me. We seemed to have a lot in common, and I told Jeanette about her. I said I thought maybe before we got any more serious I should find out how I felt about the other girl. I married the other girl within a year of the time I met her. We were pinned in three months, engaged in six months, and married in months. We've been married 52 years, so I think I made the right choice.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yes, it sounds like it.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: How did you end up getting malaria?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I have no idea. I don't know whether I got it down in Panama. I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh, you were stationed in Panama for a while?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. I was there, and --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: It doesn't take long for a mosquito to bite you.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: One mosquito to bite and you've got it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yea, that will do it.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We did have leave when we were in Panama. We were able to go into a town and see how people lived and stuff.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: My mother is from Panama.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, is that right?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I have a niece who married a guy from Panama. He hates winter. He can't stand it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yeah, I can imagine. Well -- you know, it's very interesting because my mother had never seen snow until she got married, and she liked snow, and towards the end of her life she would go back and visit her mother and she'd write back to me, I can't stand the heat here.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, Panama was kind of a backward country when I was there.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I think it always has been.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I can remember walking down the main street of the town, and it was lined with, like, shops, and the front of the thing -- the top part of the front would fold down, and these prostitutes would stand in there and try to entice you to come in, and that was the main commerce, I guess, down there then.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Was this Cristobal or Colon or --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Colon, and I didn't like it. I hated it. I was glad to ___.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did you -- were there any entertainers or did you --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, never saw any entertainer do it. I saw lots of them in movies, and I saw them on television. ___+ since I've been back, but I never saw them while I was there. They just didn't go where we went.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Well, it's -- I guess that's a problem being in the Navy. There's ___ people didn't have any -- didn't really get to see the countryside or the people.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That's right, that's right, and it would be hard, of course, with all the sailors on the ship out at sea most of the time, and we were always in a combat zone. You were always moving up towards Japan. I think it would have been very unsafe to ___ civilians at that point in time. It would have been ___. Once in a while we would have a movie. If we were in a place where we were safe we would have a movie up in the bow, and sometimes we saw the same movie over -- numerous times, and then whenever we came up alongside of another ship one of the first questions was you got any good movies? We would trade movies, and we would watch those until we got another ship.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You never got U.S. ___, I imagine on the ship?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, never. But that's all right. We understood the -- our position was such that it was not safe. We had to entertain ourselves. Most of the guys gambled away their life savings, I think, playing poker. That was about all you could do. One time we were able to tie in somehow with our radio and our captain's ___+ in the middle of the ocean, and we sat and listened to the Army-Navy game, and the Navy won, and my boss -- or our captain was so happy he broke out the beer. We all were allowed a can of beer. You weren't allowed to drink on ships.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I was just about to ask about that.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: One humorous thing happened one time. The captain -- or the officers on our ship knew there were places they probably ___+ to. What you don't see doesn't bother you, and there were a number of stills on our ship, and one of them was in the very aft of this ship, and the still blew up, and it was in the place where we kept all our P-coats which you didn't need over the Pacific so they were all stored in ___. Well, when the still blew up all the P-coats were soaked with alcohol. We had to take them all up on deck and air them out.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: What were they using them for anyway, ___?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, they were -- well, I don't know. I was a sonar man. I was not a -- ___+ over there because they were really making the still. This is some of the old timers knew how to do it. I never inquired -- I don't think it was corn because they didn't have corn. It was denatured alcohol I guess. All I know is it would eat your stomach out -- too much of it. That was not official.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yes, I --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: If the captain ___ that they would have --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Was anybody injured when the still blew up?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, no. It was way in the back of the ship, what they call a fantail of the ship.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: And nobody was taking care of it. They just let it be.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, there were people who would go in and check it periodically, see --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: But they weren't sitting next to it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, they weren't sitting next to it when it blew up.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: But that must have been a pretty large supply of beer the captain ___ for all the guys.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, that's -- there's not much that a destroyer carries. There was oil, your ammunition, there was people, there was food, and ___ booze for the officers. So, he must have had a supply stashed away.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Do you recall when your service ended? How long did it take -- I've heard stories that it takes forever to get home from some of these places.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, as I mentioned our ship was decommissioned after the war. We went to Charleston, South Carolina and the ship was decommissioned there. Put in moth balls they used to call it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And then the whole ship was sealed so that in the event of another war all you have to do is take off the seal except -- it was like putting in ___+ once -- you had to do things with the ammunition. We had to take all the ammunition off. All the records were taken off and sent somewhere else. There were a bunch of things that had to be done, and because of -- at that point in time I was then a quartermaster. I was no longer a sonar man. When the war ended you didn't need a sonar man. You didn't have any subs to chase, so they changed my grade, and when I finished with that I still had some time to go. My six months weren't up, so I was sent to another destroyer to put that one out of commission, and that's the one where I got the appendicitis and they thought I was trying to shirk my duties ___+. But the ship was called the Stoddard -- the U.S.S. Stoddard, and when I was in college my roommate was a young high school graduate, and he used to love to ask me questions about my time on the ship and the war and things like that. He was going to become a minister also, and when he graduated from college he was assigned a church in Philadelphia, and then I kind of lost track of him, and I found out that he joined the Navy as a chaplain.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You inspired him?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I apparently did. My wife and I -- I had a business trip out to California, and I took my wife with me. I had to go to both San Diego and Los Angeles -- or San Francisco and Los Angeles -- and we got down to Los Angeles and I said let's go down to San Diego and see Jack. So, Jack was my roommate and his wife was my wife's little sister in college. We introduced her. And, so we went down to visit him in San Diego, and he had all these ships up on the wall he had served on. He retired as a captain in the Navy which is one step below admiral. He did very well for himself. And all these ships were up on the wall -- pictures of them, and one of them was the Stoddard. I said Jack, I said, I knew you were always interested in my Navy experiences, but I didn't know that you were so impressed you put a picture of my ship up there. He said I was on that ship. When they re-commissioned the ship for the Korean war he went on the Stoddard -- ended up on the same ship ___ coincidence.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, he retired from Navy. Did he retire from the ministry too?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. He was a Navy chaplain.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Did he do anything in the civilian ministry.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: He started as a civilian minister, but he retired as a Navy captain, and he was second in command, I think, of the ___ chaplains ___. He had written a book which I have a copy of.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Did you keep a diary while you were out there or anything?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: There were a couple of fellows who did. In fact, I brought along with me one of those -- I have a book that was written by one of my crew members, and he kept a diary -- a book ___ everyday events. If you read his diary you'll have a pretty good idea of what happened ___+. In fact, reading his diary he reminded me of things that I had forgotten that happened. It brought back a lot of memories.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You didn't take pictures, did you?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I didn't, no. Interesting enough, and I probably should have put this in the form of a record, but the son of the captain of the Arizona, Van Valkenburgh, was assigned to our ship, and he was a lieutenant junior grade, I think. He was one of the most incompetent people I've ever met. Arrogant, haunting, unfriendly. A by-the-book kind of a man. And, in fact, he had some bad habits. One time the other officers had to take him in the shower. They stripped his clothes off, and they drove him down with a brush, Navy ___, but he was a photographer on our ship. That's -- I mean, there's the lieutenant being the ship's photographer. That's usually the job of a third class petty officer or somebody, but they didn't know what else to do with the guy. He turned out not to be very good at anything.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I take it he achieved the position because he was his father's son?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes, that's exactly right. When we got to the end of the war they had somebody else taking pictures. I don't know who did it, but I have pictures of our being in Sasebo, pictures of some of the Japanese ships there. I have pictures of our captain going onboard at the time of the surrender. I have pictures of Nagasaki, but they're very poor pictures, very poor quality. I mean, they're poor now because they're quite old and faded, but if anybody could do anything with them I'd be happy to put them out. I brought everything because I didn't know -- are you going judge whether to --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh, I'm not a judge of these things. I'm sure if possible if we could copy them maybe we could send them.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Here are some pictures of Nagasaki. As you can see, the smoke is still coming up, and it was --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Where was that one building that remained?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: It was a cement building. Apparently the cement withstood the bomb better than a lot of other things did. Metal was all twisted and stuff like that. There's another one.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: ___ some restoration, doesn't it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Now, these were ones you took or the actual photographer of your ship did?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I don't know who took them because our official photographer ___ ended up not even doing that I don't think. "U.S. Government Researchers in 1945 found radiation in the Nagasaki, Japan area that was about twice the level now considered safe for nuclear workers."

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: And that level keeps going down, down, down.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. "Reports found in the national achieves by the Washington Post will probably increase the controversy over whether U.S. soldiers sent to Nagasaki --" They're all so ___. They never talk about it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: -- "sent to NAGOSOKI and Hiroshima in 1945 absorbed enough radiation to cause cancers that appeared after 20 years or more." Well, I got out in 1946, and I started getting cancer in the eighties.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: What's the date on this?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, this is way back.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I knew a soldier who had gone to --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Here's the bikini that so amplified the fifties. A soft cup bra for $13.50. A Lady Lang bra is $15.50. An underwire bra was $13.50, and a brief is $6.50. Now, how long ago was that? And that was in the ___, so you know that's old.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: You know that's pretty old, yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Here are some pictures of just ordinary happenings. The coxswain bringing the whale boat alongside. That's the kind of thing that broke his leg and caused his death.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: There's a picture of my ship. Here's the captain going aboard a Japanese ship.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Accepting their surrender?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, I don't -- I'm not sure if he was serving a surrender or making sure that the ship was not going to be able to surreptitiously start another war. There's two of the captains -- or two of the officers of my ship. He has Alzheimer's. He's dead. Here we are -- a picture aboard a Japanese submarine. Here's another destroyer -- my destroyer that is. Here's a Japanese destroyer.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You didn't have to ___+?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Just figure your memory will do it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I just memorized them. Here's a couple of Japanese aircraft carriers, the hulks of -- this was the commandant of our fleet -- you know, of the destroyer squad rather.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Uh-huh. He was the superior of your captain?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: He was the superior of my captain. It was because of him my captain never made admiral. He gave my captain an order one time and the captain thought it was a bad order. The captain refused to do it. The commandant said I'm the commandant for this group -- whatever we called ourselves, I forget -- and the captain said that's true, but this is my ship. I'm in charge of this ship and I'm not going to do that. So, my captain never made -- because that went into his personal folder, and he never made admiral, and he was a great example. About the only man I think I ever really worshiped. There's some people down in the Philippines. Here's a front shot of our ship and right here is where I used to do my --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Looking --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: My lookout work, right there. In fact, when we were shooting at kamikaze planes these guns, of course, would be all over the place.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: They'd swing around?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Swing around, but they would go off almost in my ear when they were shooting midships.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Have you suffered any ___?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I have a lot of --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: My brother was in the maritime service, and he got his eardrums broken. He had to man a gun every once in a while.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: My wife accuses me of being deafer than I was.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Well, I'm sure that can get worse with age.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yeah, with age, right. Here is one of the harbors at Sasebo, and some of the Japanese shipping that was in it. This is another shot of the Philippines. Here's a dodo bird. That's from the island of --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: They're extinct.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, whatever it was they used to --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: That looks like a gannot (ph).

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We didn't know. We called them dodo birds. Here's the captain speaking to the crew, and I don't know what about. I don't know if I'm on these pictures or not. I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Let's see. Dinner will be served any minute now.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: This fellow here was -- right here --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: -- was a -- almost a nerd-ish looking guy. He was a medical corpsman on our ship, third class. He was one of the most heroic people you'd ever hope to meet.
