sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: He --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Heroic.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Oh, heroic, yes.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: He risked his life many times to save people, and he saved a lot of lives. We had a -- we were alongside of a landing craft one time, and it got hit by a Japanese plane. It was sinking, and it was loaded with ammunition and Marines, and he went over and treated the Marines on a ship that was about to blow up. We shot down a Japanese plane one time, and the pilot survived. He was out in the ocean all by himself, and everybody was saying let him drown. He got on a boat and went out and saved his life. I mean, he was just -- you'd look at him and you'd never believe it.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: He's still alive. I saw him last month. We had a ship's reunion, and -- wonderful guy, wonderful guy. Here's the moving thing when I said we had movies.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: There was a screen.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: If a high wind came up that would go down, wouldn't it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: It probably would have, yeah. There's my captain. I loved him, and I saw his -- we went down -- my wife and I went down and spent the weekend -- yeah, three days -- with his wife. We're very, very close to his wife.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: He died?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: He died. He died a couple years ago. I used to be up on the bridge with him all the time because sometimes when I wasn't on lookout, which is right on the bridge, he'd come up and be walking around. I was also the helmsman sometimes when I was the one who'd be steering the ship. I got to know him quite a bit, see him in different -- different roles -- and I just admired him so much. He was an Annapolis graduate. These are places -- I'm not exactly sure where they are. Here we are back in the Philippines and the huts and people are really interesting, and here we are -- I think this is me right here. We were going to pass something from our ship to this other destroyer. Whether it was movie, whether it was oil, we were taking on fuel, whether somebody was going to be going over there for some reason or what I don't remember. This is how we used to get back and forth between ships. We'd have to go by rope.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: They call that a bosun's chair?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah, a bosun's chair, and once in a while you'd get your rear end wet.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I can imagine.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Which was scary because --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Now, this was you -- the back of you in --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I think it was, but I'm not sure. I could tell you better if I saw the front. I think it was.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: So, you do have reunions from your ship?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We meet every year. Some ships meet every five years. We decided we were going to meet every year because we were dying off so fast that we figured if we waited every five years all of a sudden there wouldn't be anybody to meet. Here was a picture I brought of my boot camp. I'm there.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Ah, these are ____.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Now, where do you -- do you rotate where you meet for your reunion?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yes. We always go to different places. As a matter of fact, I talked yesterday to the visitors bureau. They're going to send material for me because I have been suggesting they come to Rochester. They don't want to come because of the weather here, it's too cold. Some of these people live down south, never lived up north.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: They're just afraid of the weather.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: What time of year do you normally have it?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: They remember boot camp.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yeah, I know.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We usually meet in October.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: October, okay. October's not too bad.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: There's a story on this one. I don't know how much you want to hear. It's not very heroic, but --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: That's you in the middle?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That's me -- yeah, that's me in the middle.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I guess ___+ the eyebrows.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And I told --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: I remember the story of that picture.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: This picture?

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Yes. He told me this picture.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: We were on our way back to the States from the war, and our ship and all the other ships that came back with us -- destroyers -- we were all survivors of different squadrons, and our ships -- the tops of our ships were all painted black, and the word got back to Hawaii -- to the shore patrol -- that the Black-top Squad -- because that's what they started calling us -- was coming in. They had been out a long time, there was probably going to be a lot of drinking, and a lot of things happening, be on the lookout for them, and don't take an awful lot from them. Well, this guy here and I were close friends -- he and I -- and we decided that we would go in and do some shopping. We got -- there was only one night that we were in Hawaii on the way back, and they told us that if we weren't back at the ship at 5 o'clock in the morning they would leave us, and that we would have to get assigned to another ship going back out in the Pacific. So, we went to go shopping, and we went to a bar and ordered a beer. We were going to have a beer before we started shopping, and the guy wouldn't serve us because we were too young to drink. You can imagine telling that to a couple of sailors who just came back from almost two years of combat. So, we went to another bar to get a beer, and they wouldn't serve us there. We were getting frustrated at that point and a little upset, and as we were walking down the street discussing this matter this guy came along who was a lot older than we. We hardly even knew him. I still don't really know him, but he talked to us for a while and found out we were -- he said I'll get you a drink. He came back with a bottle of whiskey, and then the three of us sat down for some stupid reason and finished the bottle of whiskey, and we got quite drunk, and before long we were arrested by the shore patrol, put in the brig, and told that they would release us at 7 o'clock the following morning. That's when the released their prisoners. You can imagine what that does to somebody who's on his way home, and then suddenly finds out he may be going back out in the opposite direction. So, anyway, 7 o'clock in the morning -- and I didn't know what I was going to do, nor did anybody else frankly, and I can't remember exactly what time it was, but it was about -- between 4:30 and quarter of five -- we got the word that they were coming to pick us up, and each ship has a landing craft out there to carry their crew back to their ship. The reason they did that was because there were so many sailors from our group in the brig they didn't have enough to sail the ship back to the United States, so they had to get us anyway. And this picture here was taken in the Philippines. I went down and met a buddy of mine -- there's another story. I was a runner in high school. I was a state champion in at least one kind of track, and three other fellows and myself were a relay team and set a record that lasted for about four years in the state of Pennsylvania, and Mother was so proud of me, and she always kept saying I hope you never smoke, never smoke, never smoke. We were in the Philippines. I saw my buddy's ship, and I went over to visit with him, and one of his officers took a picture of us -- of me alone, him alone, both of us together, and all that. He's dead now, too.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: You didn't send this home to your mother, did you?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, I didn't, but he sent them home to his sister, and his sister saw my mother and said oh, I got some pictures, let me show you. Mother never mentioned it, never said a thing about it, but the day I got home they picked me up at the railroad station, and on the way home from the railroad station Mother said I see you're smoking. I'm glad you're home. That's the story of that picture and the other one.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Are you still a smoker?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. If you'd had as many cancers as I've had you don't want -- you don't need anymore. There's a picture of me -- you talked about having pictures. Again, I don't know what you could use.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: A formal picture.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That's more formal. Here's a picture of my folks and me standing in front of our house.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Your brother?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Of me.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Oh, I thought you said ___.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I have pictures of my brother and I too in uniform, but I didn't bring them. This is my story, not his.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: You should talk to him and see if his --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Where is he?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: He lives in Fort Myers, Florida.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: ___+ if he might want to --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Participate, right.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: He had a wife who got Alzheimer's and he cared for her himself for eight years. Fed her, ___ her, dressed her, and never was going to marry again, and then he met a wonderful woman, and he married her.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Well, that's good.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: And they moved to Florida. Okay, anything else you want to know? Is there something special --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: To get back to your reunions, how many men are left from your ship?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: At the last one I think we had 25.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Out of?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Maybe 35. Between 25 and 35.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: How many men originally?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: 330. I brought all this stuff along because I didn't know what you might want. At our last reunion they gave out a list of all of our crew, those who were dead, those who they hadn't been able to locate, and those who were still attending the -- those that we had located and weren't coming, and those that were coming. Most of us are dead. There is a book -- there are a series of books called -- one of them -- the first one is called The Sacrificial Lambs Who Fought Like Lions, the U.S. Destroyers Versus Japanese kamikazes, and there are a lot of pictures in here that -- here's a suicide plane coming in here, and here's a crew shooting at it. So, as you can see, he's coming right over the water.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Yeah. It's so frightening.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: This is what's left of a lot of these ships when they'd been hit. These are all destroyers that were out on the picket lines. As you can imagine, everybody up here was killed. Some of the ships -- everybody in the back -- well, we would come up along side of them as they were sinking, and we would take as many of their live people over as possible, many of whom were so badly wounded. The first time this ever happened -- and that was with the ship that I mentioned the captain told them that they were going to be under attack, get out of the way -- that ship, they brought all their -- as they were sinking they brought the survivors over to our ship. I tried to help with the wounded, and there were so many people badly burned, some of them were just coated black ___+. The smell and the screams, it was horrible. I couldn't do it. I went to the back of the ship and threw up over the side. That was my first experience with this kind of thing, but as you can well imagine --

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: I imagine those people didn't survive?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No. Most of them died.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Were there -- but there were people who were able to help them?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, although I have to admit that I didn't help very much. That was my first experience with it, and I didn't handle it at all well. I don't seem to do very well in first experiences.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Does anybody?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: That's the kind of a ship I was on. That is my ship there. This is about destroyers, not just about my ship. This is what we looked like.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: It is right over the water, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Yeah. There's one-quarter inch of steel between us and the water -- a quarter inch, that's it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: Which isn't much.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: That doesn't seem like -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: So, these ships, when they get hit, are really bad. And, again, that's where I would be; up there, up here.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: There is no crow's nest anymore, is there?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: No, no. Not with radar there isn't. Although, interestingly enough, the Navy wasn't ready for radar. Our ship was built without radar. It was designed without radar because radar hadn't been developed at that point at which the ship was designed. When it became necessary to start putting radar on the ships the ships became top heavy, and some of them went down. In fact, we were right near one coming back to Bermuda one time.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hannon
sp.p: It capsized?

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: It capsized. We were in a storm off the coast of Norfolk, Virginia, and that's known for its storms. So --

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: Well, we're almost out of tape, I think, and I think we've in a round about way covered a majority of the questions, but is there --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: I don't know exactly what you're going to do with this.

sp.speaker: Annette Goodman
sp.p: -- anything else you want to add about -- that we haven't covered about your experiences or your life afterwards of how you were treated afterwards as a veteran or --

sp.speaker: Laverne C. Etshman
sp.p: Well, I did go to college. I majored in psychology. I played soccer for the college. I got to be a very good soccer player. I'd never seen a game until I got into college. I used to be a runner, as I said, and I went out for soccer to get in shape for track, and we sat through four games, and I was on the bench, and we were getting beaten by just about every school. We were playing the Lehigh University -- no it was Temple -- and my coach turned to me, and he says, could you do that because we had just had another goal scored against us. He wanted to know could I be a goalie. I said I don't know, I'll try it. So, I went into the second half and they didn't score against me, and from that point on we didn't get scored against very often, so I got to be the goalie for the team. We were middle Atlantic champions by the time I graduated. I was a member of a fraternity. I was elected to the National Honorary Fraternity. That was lamb-dah -- I forget the -- you know, it's funny. I go back to pick something up, and I don't always remember it. But anyway, it was a national leadership society fraternity. I had a lot of different -- (END OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE)
